name: ZAMBIA

flag.title: Flag of Zambia
flag.note: Green with orange eagle, red & black stripes

lead: Landlocked in the heart of Africa, Zambia is draped in savannah and forest. The Zambezi River plunges 108 m over Victoria Falls in a curtain of thunder and mist. Zambia won freedom from Britain in 1964, naming itself after that river. With 20 national parks, it is one of Africa's greatest wildlife destinations.
geo: Zambia sits on a high plateau averaging 1,200 m — so even near the equator it stays pleasant. Three great rivers cross it: the Zambezi, the Kafue, and the Luangwa. Lake Tanganyika, one of the world's deepest lakes, touches its northern border.

Victoria Falls — locally Mosi-oa-Tunya, 'the smoke that thunders' — straddles the Zimbabwe border. Spray rises 400 m in flood season, visible 50 km away. The vast Bangweulu Swamps in the north shelter the rare shoebill stork.
animals: Zambia protects wildlife across 20 national parks. South Luangwa is famous for walking safaris — tracking lions and leopards on foot. Kafue National Park is the size of Switzerland, sheltering wild dogs, cheetahs, and vast buffalo herds.

The Zambezi teems with hippos and crocodiles. The Bangweulu Swamps harbour the shoebill — a massive grey bird that stands motionless for hours. Zambia also hosts the Thornicroft's giraffe, a rare subspecies found nowhere else on Earth.
culture: Zambia has 70+ ethnic groups yet is famed for unity — the motto is 'One Zambia, One Nation'. Music and dance anchor every celebration. Each February the Ngoni perform Nc'wala, giving thanks for the harvest with warrior dances and drumming.

Food centres on nshima — thick maize porridge eaten by rolling a ball and dipping it into fish, beans, or greens. Chitenge — boldly patterned cloth — is worn as skirts, slings, and headscarves, turning every market into a blaze of colour.
history: Before Europeans arrived, the Lozi kingdom ruled the fertile Barotse floodplain and the Bemba held the north. David Livingstone reached Victoria Falls in 1855; by 1924 the territory became British-ruled Northern Rhodesia.

Zambia won independence on 24 October 1964, with Kenneth Kaunda as first president, and renamed itself after the Zambezi. Copper brought wealth; falling prices in the 1970s caused hardship, but growth has been steady since the 1990s.
wows: Victoria Falls is 1,708 m wide — the world's largest by width and height combined.
The Zambia–Zimbabwe border runs right through the middle of the falls.
Kafue National Park covers 22,400 km² — larger than the whole of Wales.
Zambia was among the first African nations to broadcast TV, as early as 1961.
The shoebill stork stands over 1.5 m tall with a beak shaped like a wooden clog.
Zambezi rapids below the falls are Class 5 — the maximum survivable grade.
Zambia holds over 40% of Africa's surface fresh water within its borders.

myths.myth: Zambia is dry desert or scrubland
myths.fact: Zambia is about 65% forest and woodland, crossed by three major rivers and vast wetlands. Its high-plateau climate is mild and green for much of the year.

myths.myth: Victoria Falls belongs only to Zimbabwe
myths.fact: The falls straddle both countries equally. Zambia's town of Livingstone sits right on the bank and offers the best full-width view of the cascade.
